lesson.title: What Makes a Technology "General Purpose"
lesson.summary: Introduces the General Purpose Technology (GPT) framework ,  the three-part test economists use to identify technologies capable of reshaping an entire economy ,  using steam power, electricity, and transistors as illustrations.
lesson.body:
Most inventions solve one problem for one group of users. A better plow helps farmers; a faster loom helps weavers. But every so often, an invention comes along that doesn't stay in its lane ,  it gets pulled into industries nobody expected, keeps getting better for decades, and drags a wave of other inventions along with it. Economists call these general purpose technologies, or GPTs, and they built a specific three-part test to identify them rather than just calling anything "revolutionary."

The first criterion is pervasiveness: a true GPT ends up used across a wide range of unrelated sectors, not just the industry it was invented for. The second is continuous improvement: its performance or cost keeps getting better over a long stretch of time, rather than plateauing quickly the way most inventions do. The third, and the one people find hardest to picture, is that it spawns complementary innovations ,  it creates opportunities for other people to invent things that only make sense once the core technology exists. These three properties reinforce each other. As a technology gets cheaper or more capable, more sectors find a use for it (pervasiveness feeds off improvement). As more sectors adopt it, more people are exposed to its quirks and limitations, which gives them reasons to invent workarounds and extensions (pervasiveness feeds complementary innovation). And those new complementary inventions often create fresh demand that funds further improvement of the core technology. The transformation isn't caused by the invention itself; it's caused by this loop running for decades.

Electricity is the textbook case. On its own, a generator just converts mechanical motion into current ,  useful, but not obviously world-changing. What made it a GPT was that it turned out to be equally relevant to lighting, to running factory machinery, to refrigeration, and to communication, so it spread into essentially every sector (pervasiveness). Generation and transmission efficiency kept climbing for the better part of a century (continuous improvement). And its presence made possible things that had never existed before ,  the electric motor let factories abandon the single central steam engine driving pulleys throughout the building, which let engineers redesign factory floors around workflow instead of proximity to the power source (complementary innovation). None of those three things alone would have transformed manufacturing; together, they did.

The steam engine and the transistor follow the same pattern for the same underlying reason: a technology that only improves in isolation, or only serves one industry, or never inspires anything built on top of it, simply cannot generate economy-wide change no matter how impressive it looks in its original application. The transistor, for instance, wasn't just a smaller vacuum tube ,  it kept shrinking and cheapening for decades, showed up in everything from calculators to communications infrastructure, and enabled entirely new industries like software that had no reason to exist beforehand.

Holding a candidate technology up against these three criteria ,  pervasive use, sustained improvement, and downstream innovation it enables ,  gives you a disciplined way to ask whether the hype matches the mechanism. That's exactly the test you'll apply to quantum computing throughout the rest of this book.
